---
title: "Multi-Omics Integration"
description: "Strategies for combining genotype, expression, methylation, and other data types measured on the same samples."
---

Papers on how to analyse several data types (genotypes, gene expression, DNA
methylation, and so on) measured on the same samples together, rather than one
at a time.

## Ritchie et al. (2015): Methods of integrating data to uncover genotype–phenotype interactions

Ritchie MD, Holzinger ER, Li R, Pendergrass SA, Kim D. Methods of integrating
data to uncover genotype–phenotype interactions. *Nature Reviews Genetics*
16(2), 85–97 (2015).

- [doi:10.1038/nrg3868](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrg3868) (paywalled)
- [PDF in lab-papers](https://github.com/Omnia-Lab-UC/lab-papers/blob/main/ritchie-2015-integrating-data-genotype-phenotype.pdf)
  (lab members only)

**Why read it.** A review that sorts integration methods into two families.
*Multi-staged* analysis works through the data types one step at a time, for
example from SNPs to gene expression to phenotype. *Meta-dimensional* analysis
combines all the data types in a single analysis, and comes in three forms:

- **Concatenation-based:** join the feature matrices of all data types into one
  matrix and model that.
- **Transformation-based:** turn each data type into an intermediate form, such
  as a graph or kernel matrix, and combine those.
- **Model-based:** build a model for each data type separately and combine the
  models.

**Focus on.** The meta-dimensional section. [SNF](similarity-network-fusion.qmd)
is a transformation-based method: each data type becomes a patient similarity
network, and the networks are fused instead of the raw features. The trade-offs
the review describes for each family are the ones you'll need when you explain
why we chose that approach.

## Rappoport & Shamir (2018): Multi-omic and multi-view clustering algorithms: review and cancer benchmark

Rappoport N, Shamir R. Multi-omic and multi-view clustering algorithms: review
and cancer benchmark. *Nucleic Acids Research* 46(20), 10546–10562 (2018).

- [doi:10.1093/nar/gky889](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gky889)
- [Free full text on PubMed Central (PMC6237755)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6237755/)
- [Benchmark scripts on GitHub](https://github.com/Shamir-Lab/Multi-Omics-Cancer-Benchmark)

**Why read it.** A review of clustering methods for multi-omics data, followed
by a benchmark. The review groups methods into early integration (concatenate
the omics and cluster the result), late integration (cluster each omic
separately, then combine the solutions), and intermediate integration (one model
over all omics). Intermediate methods are further split into similarity-based
methods, which include SNF, dimension-reduction methods, and statistical models.
The benchmark runs nine methods, SNF among them, on gene expression, DNA
methylation, and miRNA expression for ten TCGA cancer types. It scores each
solution on survival differences between clusters and on enrichment of clinical
labels.

Two results to keep in mind. No method beat all the others, and multi-omics
clustering did not consistently do better than clustering a single omic. Also,
the usual chi-squared approximation of the logrank p-value was inaccurate with
small samples and unbalanced cluster sizes, so the authors recommend
permutation-based p-values instead.

**Focus on.** The similarity-based methods part of the review, and the Benchmark
and Discussion sections. Read them before you choose which methods to compare
SNF against and how to evaluate the clusters. The rest of the review is a
reference to come back to when another method comes up.
